title: The Peer Problem Nobody Teaches You to Solve
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: Lead With Kelly argues that peer dynamics -- the relationships between leaders at the same level -- are the most politically loaded and least-studied dimension of organizational leadership, with an entire library written on managing up and managing down but almost nothing on managing sideways. The article opens with a personal failure: the author tried to drive a cross-company finance transformation without investing in peer relationships first, pushing hard on what needed to change without making colleagues want to change alongside her. The lesson: 'your success depends far less on the team you manage and much more on the team you sit with.' The article classifies peer archetypes into three types: The Competitor (in implicit competition for the next role, expressing it through subtle information delays, credit absorption, resource withholding); The Collaborator (rare, argues with you in meetings but backs you in private, genuinely aligned on enterprise outcomes); and The Lone Wolf (not competing, not collaborating, simply surviving -- dangerous precisely because they look fine but undermine cross-team alignment). The article closes with a critique of the 'align offline' coping mechanism as a way peer conflict rots rather than resolves.
points: Peer dynamics are the most politically loaded and least-taught dimension of leadership: shared ambition, shared resources, and zero formal authority over one another create distinctive relational challenges that almost no management literature directly addresses.

The Competitor archetype is not about open rivalry but subtle expressions: information shared a beat late, credit absorbed for shared work, resources held slightly longer -- patterns that most teams pretend don't exist but almost always do.

The Lone Wolf archetype is dangerous precisely because it looks fine on the surface: delivers the numbers, causes no drama, but is absent from the cross-team alignment work that the peer team requires to actually move.

The 'align offline' coping mechanism -- sidebar after a meeting disagreement, united front next time without resolving anything -- is a way for peer conflict to rot rather than resolve, and a sophisticated form of avoidance.

Turning a Lone Wolf requires demonstrating that you can make their life easier -- once they trust that, the door to genuine collaboration opens, but appeals to team spirit before that trust exists will not work.
quotes: Your success depends far less on the team you manage and much more on the team you sit with. The peer team shapes the decisions, guards the culture, and sets the tone that every other team in the organization watches and follows.

On the surface, we were polite. Underneath, we were stuck. The real conversations happened after the meeting. In the room, everyone nodded. After the room, everyone disagreed. Nothing moved because nothing real was said where it mattered.
Until then, I had considered myself to be a leader of my function. After that, I understood I was a leader of the enterprise, and my function was just where my desk happened to sit.
The Collaborator is rare. When you find one, invest deeply. Most senior careers are built on a small number of these relationships.
You don't turn them by talking to them about the team. You turn them by genuinely demonstrating that you can make their life easier. Once they trust that, the door opens.

We didn't have a strategy problem. We didn't have a talent problem. We had a leadership team problem, and the cost was being paid everywhere downstream by people who could sense that their managers weren't actually aligned.
